pharm: A trihydroxamic-acid siderophore that binds free iron (and aluminum) to form the water-soluble, renally excreted complex ferrioxamine, removing iron not bound to transferrin/hemoglobin and promoting its urinary and biliary excretion.
quick: Chronic overload: 20-40 mg/kg/day SC/IV infusion over 8-24 h; acute poisoning: 15 mg/kg/h IV (max ~6-8 g/day)
Parenteral; not related to meals (vitamin C may be given separately to enhance excretion)
Use only if clearly needed; acute iron poisoning is itself a major fetal threat
Caution; excretion in milk unknown - decide to stop drug or nursing
Renally cleared as ferrioxamine; use cautiously and monitor; consider dialysis if anuric
Annual ophthalmologic and audiometric exams, growth in children, serum ferritin, renal function
summary: Deferoxamine mesylate is a parenteral iron-chelating agent indicated for acute iron intoxication and chronic iron overload from transfusion-dependent anemias (e.g. thalassemia). It binds ferric iron to form ferrioxamine, which is excreted in the urine (turning it a characteristic reddish/orange color) and bile. It does not bind iron in transferrin, hemoglobin, or cytochromes. Long-term use can cause dose-related ocular toxicity (retinal/optic changes, night blindness, visual field/color defects) and ototoxicity (high-frequency hearing loss), so periodic eye and hearing exams are required. Rapid intravenous infusion can cause hypotension, flushing, urticaria, and shock; in chronic use ARDS has occurred with very high doses. It also chelates aluminum and is used in aluminum overload of dialysis patients. Pulmonary, growth, and infection risks (Yersinia, Mucormycosis) require monitoring.
indications: Chronic iron overload due to transfusion-dependent anemias (e.g. thalassemia major)
Aluminum overload in patients with end-stage renal disease on dialysis (off-label/established use per label discussion)

dosage.d: IV infusion 15 mg/kg/hour; reduce rate after 4-6 h; total usually not exceeding 6 g (up to 8 g) in 24 h
dosage.n: IV is the route of choice in patients with cardiovascular collapse/shock; titrate to clinical response and urine color

dosage.c: Acute iron poisoning (IM where IV not feasible)
dosage.d: Initial 1000 mg, then 500 mg every 4 h for 2 doses; subsequent 500 mg every 4-12 h
dosage.n: Max about 6 g/24 h; IM only if not in shock

dosage.d: 20-40 mg/kg/day (commonly up to ~40-60 mg/kg) by slow SC infusion over 8-12 (up to 24) h via portable pump, 5-7 nights/week
dosage.n: Average daily dose should not exceed 40 mg/kg in adults; titrate to ferritin and 24-h urine iron

dosage.d: May give with each transfusion or as slow IV infusion; do not exceed 15 mg/kg/hour
dosage.n: Do not give the entire daily dose as a rapid bolus

dosage.d: Limit average daily dose to 40 mg/kg until growth ceased; doses >60 mg/kg associated with toxicity
dosage.n: Monitor growth and bone (growth retardation and bone changes with high doses)

admin: Reconstitute with sterile water for injection; for SC use give as a slow infusion over 8-24 hours with a portable pump
For IV use infuse slowly - do NOT push rapidly (rapid IV causes hypotension, flushing, urticaria, shock)
IM is an alternative route for acute poisoning only if the patient is not in shock
Inspect injection site; subcutaneous infusion can cause local irritation, induration, and erythema
Warn that urine may turn a reddish/orange (vin rose) color - this is expected and indicates iron excretion
Obtain baseline ophthalmologic and audiometric exams before long-term therapy and repeat periodically
moa: Deferoxamine is a hydroxylamine-derivative siderophore that chelates iron by forming a stable octahedral complex with ferric iron (Fe3+). One molecule binds one atom of iron; 100 mg of deferoxamine can theoretically bind about 8.5 mg of ferric iron. It has high affinity for free iron and for iron in ferritin and hemosiderin, but does NOT remove iron from transferrin, hemoglobin, or cytochrome-bound (functional) iron. The resulting complex, ferrioxamine, is water-soluble and is excreted mainly by the kidneys (giving urine a reddish color) and partly in bile/feces. Deferoxamine also chelates aluminum, forming aluminoxamine that is dialyzable, which underlies its use in dialysis-related aluminum overload.

absolute: Severe renal disease or anuria (relative/absolute - it and its iron complex are renally excreted), unless dialysis available
relative: Patients at risk of Yersinia or Mucormycosis infection
monitor: Ophthalmologic status (retina, optic nerve, visual fields, color and night vision)
Growth and bone development in children

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; deferoxamine has shown skeletal anomalies in animals at high doses. In acute iron poisoning, however, untreated iron toxicity poses a serious risk to both mother and fetus, so deferoxamine should be used when clearly indicated. Use during the first trimester only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: It is not known whether deferoxamine is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in milk and because of the potential for adverse reactions, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Deferoxamine and its iron complex (ferrioxamine) are eliminated by the kidneys. In patients with renal impairment iron-chelate may accumulate; use with caution and monitor renal function. In anuric patients or severe renal disease the drug should generally be avoided or given only with dialysis (ferrioxamine and aluminoxamine are dialyzable). Aluminum overload chelation in dialysis patients is timed to dialysis.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment for hepatic impairment is provided in the labeling; deferoxamine is largely excreted renally. Monitor as clinically indicated.

major: Prochlorperazine - concurrent use may lead to temporary impairment of consciousness
Gallium-67 imaging - deferoxamine can distort results; discontinue 48 hours before scintigraphy
moderate: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) - increases availability of iron for chelation and urinary iron excretion but can worsen tissue iron toxicity and cardiac dysfunction; give only after the first month of regular deferoxamine, with caution in cardiac disease
interactions.food: No clinically significant food interaction; vitamin C supplementation should be limited and given cautiously (see above).
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction with alcohol is described in the labeling.
interactions.diagnostics: May interfere with gallium-67 scintigraphy (discontinue 48 h before). Urine turns reddish from iron-deferoxamine complex; this is a normal pharmacologic effect, not a lab abnormality.

common: Injection-site reactions (pain, induration, erythema, swelling, pruritus)
serious: Ocular toxicity - blurred vision, cataracts, decreased visual acuity, night blindness, visual field defects, retinopathy, optic neuritis
Ototoxicity - high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus
Hypotension, tachycardia, and shock with rapid IV infusion
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with excessively high IV doses
Growth retardation and bone (metaphyseal) changes in children
rare: Seizures (especially in dialysis patients on concomitant aluminum chelation)

monitoring: Ophthalmologic examination (slit-lamp, fundoscopy, visual fields, color and night vision) at baseline and at least annually
Audiometry at baseline and periodically (every 3-12 months)
Serum ferritin and 24-hour urinary iron excretion to guide dosing
Growth and bone development in children (height, X-ray of spine/long bones)
Vigilance for Yersinia infection (fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea) and fungal (Mucormycosis) infection
counsel: Your urine may turn a reddish or orange color while on this medicine - this is normal and shows iron is being removed
For subcutaneous use, the medicine is given slowly through a small pump, usually overnight; rotate injection sites
Keep all eye and hearing test appointments - this medicine can affect vision and hearing if levels are too high
Report any blurred vision, trouble seeing at night, ringing in the ears, or hearing loss promptly
Tell your doctor about fever, abdominal pain, or diarrhea - certain infections need the medicine stopped temporarily
Do not take large vitamin C supplements unless your doctor advises - it can worsen iron-related heart problems
pk: Iron binding is rapid after infusion begins; urinary iron excretion within hours
Plasma levels peak during/at end of infusion (drug is given by infusion)
Distribution ~5-10 minutes; deferoxamine ~6 hours; ferrioxamine longer
Short - continuous or prolonged infusion needed to sustain chelation
Store dry powder below 25 C; use reconstituted solution promptly (discard if cloudy)
pearls: Classic triad of chronic toxicity to watch: OCULAR (retinopathy/optic), AUDITORY (high-frequency hearing loss), and pulmonary (ARDS at very high IV doses)
Reddish urine ('vin rose') confirms iron is being excreted - reassure patients
Never give the daily IV dose as a rapid bolus - rapid infusion causes hypotension and shock; keep <=15 mg/kg/h
Predisposes to Yersinia enterocolitica and Mucormycosis - hold the drug and treat if these are suspected
Limit average daily dose to 40 mg/kg in adults and children (growth retardation with high doses in kids)
Also chelates aluminum (forms dialyzable aluminoxamine) - used in dialysis aluminum overload
missed: Deferoxamine is given by a healthcare team or via a prescribed pump schedule. If a scheduled subcutaneous infusion is missed, resume the next scheduled infusion as directed; do not double up. Contact your treatment center for guidance rather than changing the regimen yourself.
overdose: Acute overdose may cause hypotension, tachycardia, gastrointestinal disturbances, acute transient blindness, aphasia, agitation, bradycardia, acute renal failure, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. There is no specific antidote. Deferoxamine and ferrioxamine are dialyzable, so hemodialysis can hasten removal. Management is supportive with attention to blood pressure, renal function, and respiratory status; slow or stop the infusion.
